title: Instead of 'De-Centering the Text' Here's How to 'Re-Center' It
author: Doug Lemov
summary: This short but pointed article from Doug Lemov responds to the National Council of Teachers of English's 2022 policy statement calling for 'decentering the book' and long-form essay writing. Lemov argues that the corrective is not complicated: re-center the book. He lays out a seven-step recipe for whole-class reading practice that treats sustained shared reading as both a cognitive and social act. The approach combines teacher read-aloud, student silent reading, and shared oral reading (FASE reading), which he argues rebuilds fractured student attention by socializing sustained focus -- the same mechanism that keeps audiences in a movie theater for two hours. Vocabulary, background knowledge, and frequent short writing in response to the text complete the recipe. Lemov's argument is quietly countercultural: in an era when many practitioners are asking whether class time for sustained reading is viable, he insists not only that it is viable but that it is the primary instructional move for literacy development.
points: * The NCTE's 2022 policy statement arguing for 'decentering the book' has not been retracted in four years -- Lemov reads this as an ongoing endorsement of the view, and his response is a practical seven-step recipe for doing the opposite. * Shared oral reading (FASE reading) is described as the most important element of the re-centering approach because it makes reading a social act: just as audiences sustain attention on a film for two hours partly because everyone else in the theater is doing so, shared reading socializes states of increased focus. * Understanding is knowledge-driven more than skill-driven, which means feeding in relevant background knowledge via short nonfiction texts embedded in the reading sequence is not supplementary but central -- it provides the context that enables meaning-making. * Frequent short writing responses to the text serve to 'refine ideas and process effortfully' rather than to assess; the use of hedged prompts ('why might Jonas have responded that way?') lowers stakes while ensuring all students have developed an initial written position before discussion begins. * Close reading of small, working-memory-friendly text sections is cognitively privileged by putting the critical lines on the board for constant reference, and comparing the original to a minimally different version (a single word changed) trains students to notice how meaning shifts with precision.
quotes: Lots of belated attention over on X/Twitter for the NCTE's shameful 2022 policy statement arguing in favor of 'decentering the book' as well as long form essay writing... and presumably anything else that might be effortful for students. They've had four years to retract it and haven't, so I can only assume they still believe this to be true.

Allocate significant chunks of class time for sustained focused and, in significant part, shared reading. We can rebuild fractured student attention by causing them to practice reading for increasing periods of time.

Use a combination of teacher read aloud, student silent reading and, probably most important, shared oral reading... This process brings the book to life for students and also makes reading social. To experience a book together makes it more meaningful, but just as important, the social aspect of reading together also helps sustain attention. Students sustain their attention on a movie for two hours in part because everyone else around them in the theater is also doing so.

Feed in background knowledge as you read as well. Understanding is knowledge driven more than skill driven. Embedding short nonfiction texts to give more information about some relevant aspect of the book is the optimal way to do this.

Have students write frequently and often for short periods of time in response to the text. Make the purpose of these short responses to refine ideas and process effortfully. Words like 'might' help to lower the stakes: '45 seconds to think in writing. Why might Jonas have responded that way?' Then discuss once students have developed initial ideas in writing.
